items.content:
Couldn't agree more! A single network detection rule won't be enough to address AI-assisted attacks.

An AI agent doesn't necessarily follow a fixed execution path. If Nmap fails, it can generate a Python scanner. If an HTTP request gets blocked, it can modify its approach or switch tools while pursuing the same objective.

We've already seen threat actors experimenting with multiple AI models, assigning different roles to agents, and adapting their operations based on feedback.

Static signatures still have value, but detecting the behavior across the entire attack sequence becomes much more important.

RT @IntCyberDigest: ‼️ On a Mac, a German "ß" in a file name can slip past security checks in popular developer tools. US vulnerability centre CERT/CC warned today.

Macs can treat "ß" and "ss" as the same file. Tools from Terraform and Deno to Python's setuptools compared the letters exactly, so a blocked file gets through under the other spelling.

A local attacker could overwrite protected files or sneak secrets into uploads and software packages.

Several vendors have assigned CVEs and shipped fixes.

items.content:
RT @360_Hardware: GPT Astra ha decompilado la BIOS de mi placa base. Puedo hacer cambios en la BIOS y flashearla. Quiero intentar portear la feature SkyOC que Asrock lanzó hace años para overclockear procesadores no-K a procesadores modernos.

Los procesadores no-K se pueden overclockear subiendo el BCLK. Normalmente eso hace OC de toda la placa base, incluido RAM, buses, PCIe... pero las placas base de gama alta, suelen tener un BCLK independiente para el CPU. Por lo tanto, es técnicamente posible overclockear procesadores no-k. Sin embargo, hay un hard-limit implementado por intel, si el procesador detecta un BCLK superior a 103Mhz (el default es 100Mhz) el procesador se apaga.

Asrock encontró la forma de saltarse esta limitación engañando al procesador con un reporte falso de la frecuencia real del BCLK. Llamaron a esta feature SkyOC por que permitia overclockear procesadores Skylake. Intel les obligo a eliminar esta feature, y asrock lanzó una actualización de BIOS para eliminarla de todas sus placas base.

He mandado a GPT Astra decompilar la BIOS de asrock pre y post eliminación de SkyOC. Ha encontrado el código que permitia este truco, y ha modificado la BIOS de mi placa base para tratar de implementarlo. Veremos si funciona 🤞

items.content:
RT @MalDevAcademy: Today we released WhisperLoader, a stealthy loader that combines Thread Name-Calling for payload delivery with a TP_DIRECT.Callback hijack for execution on the victim's own pool worker thread.

The loader injects the shellcode into the target remote process using thread descriptions via APC queues, skipping PROCESS_VM_WRITE access on the process handle and skipping NtWriteVirtualMemory. If the target process already exposes a PAGE_EXECUTE_READWRITE memory region, the loader reuses it skipping both NtAllocateVirtualMemory and NtProtectVirtualMemory calls.

The shellcode is executed by hijacking a TP_DIRECT.Callback pointer inside an existing thread pool object (TP_IO / TP_ALPC / TP_JOB), then posting a single completion packet so the victim's own worker dispatches into it.

https://t.co/epouhr8B0K

items.content:
And that’s why I think people are missing the bigger picture with all these ARTEX dashboards, trackers and IoC collections.

When I first pointed at ARTEX and Cairn, it wasn’t about these two projects. It was about a tipping point we had crossed.

For a long time, autonomous pentesting agents got stuck, failed to recover from errors or kept going in circles. But something changed this late summer. Models became capable enough to overcome these obstacles, keep making progress and execute substantial parts of real intrusions with little human supervision.

That’s the development I wanted people to notice.

We’re looking at a new class of offensive systems that has suddenly become operationally viable. The individual frameworks are just examples of it.

And I expect this capability to improve and spread much faster than the names we currently associate with it.

items.content:
RT @chrisrohlf: Anthropic is making some important changes to our Coordinated Vulnerability Disclosure policy in order to keep pace with the rapid improvement of AI driven vulnerability discovery capabilities.

Starting in January we are moving to a 30-day timeline for Critical and High vulnerabilities, and 45 days for everything else. See the post linked below for more details.

We know that this change may put more pressure on OSS maintainers and vendors. Given this change some important aspects of our policy are worth calling out here:

* We will continue to agree to a sustainable pace with maintainers and vendors before sending a large volume of findings.
* We will always include a patch or mitigation with each finding where possible.
* We will work with vendors and OSS maintainers on a timeline for issues that can’t be fixed quickly.
* A reminder that issues reported with no human triage, such as those from OSS-Scanner are not subject to this policy. See our FAQ for more details.

We know that we cannot just patch our way to better security. Securing all of the code in the world requires a combination of language modernization, redesign, rewriting, hardening, reducing attack surface, and yes, finding and fixing vulnerabilities. But we must move at a faster pace together in order to make progress.

items.content:
RT @ChrisMartzWX: MYTH: Nuclear waste is a big problem.

REALITY: It’s not.

Nuclear waste byproducts are stored in steel-lined concrete casks until the fission products decay. Its radioactivity actually falls by ~99% after 40 years.

What's more, ~96% of the potential energy remains in spent nuclear fuel rods. The rods consist primarily of unused uranium-238 (~95%), a small amount of plutonium (~1%), and ~4% radioactive fission products (waste). The U.S. doesn't recycle it, but it can be done.

In any case, the photo below shows what 20 years’ worth of spent nuclear fuel looks like stored at the former Maine Yankee Nuclear Power Plant in Wiscasset, Maine.

It's a nothingburger.

items.content:
RT @0xpwnie: Ngl i didn't know about Alyssa before now and this is coming from someone who enjoys reading about top dawgs in Computer Science generally. But after hearing about the Apple M1 GPU RE I spent the past two days reading up on lady Rosenzweig. Apparently she didn't start reverse engineering GPUs this year. It was back in 2017 when she was in highschool which later turned into a Collabora job working on Panfrost(the open Mesa driver for Mali(graphics processors designed by ARM)).

This specific Apple M1 GPU work commenced in Dec of 2020, despite the fact that there weren't any publicly available docs by Apple for their GPU ISA/command stream. Hector Martin(founder of Asahi Linux) kicked off the Asahi Linux project to port the Linux operating system directly to Apple's silicon(M1 and M2 series chips). She bought herself an M1 Mac mini as a 'christmas present' and commenced work on the GPU.

Typically, it used the same black-box method as Panfrost, idk much about these really but it's a black-box reverse-engineering technique used to build open source graphics drivers without access to official documentation or source code.

After a few weeks she could disassemble simple shaders. 
Not long after she drew a triangle(drawing a triangle is the ultimate Proof of Concept in graphics engineering). You know what they say, "once you can draw a triangle, you can do anything."

Fast forward to 5 years later and we have conformant OpenGL 4.6, OpenGL ES 3.2, Vulkan 1.4,... Proton gaming works on M1 Mac running Linux(this is ridiculously insane btw).

She wrapped up the project this year and other efforts are now building on what she reverse-engineered.

items.content:
RT @GrahamHelton3: I know people are leaning towards the "lets just build all our own dependencies" as a way out of this supply chain mess we are in. I don't think this is the correct approach. 

The number one thing I look for when trying to find vulnerabilities are places where people have written their own implementation for something complex. 

Bruce Schneier famously wrote "Those who would defeat cryptography rarely attack the mathematics directly; instead, they attack the systems, networks, and humans that implement and use the security".

The same is true of most applications. I know you may think it's safer to write your own software in rust, but I promise it's going to be riddled with holes. 

A better idea would be to maintain a private fork of software you depend on. 

Even just having a policy/control that enforces a 1 week hold before pulling software would mitigate most supply chain compromises since those are picked up pretty fast.
